greeting.text: The office is empty, its shutter still open. On the muster floor, someone shouts for a stretcher; someone else shouts about a barrow, louder. Rourke's good coat still hangs on the nail. He never wore it underground.
Rourke is on the muster floor, not in the office, his arm strapped as he argues about a barrow that has not come up. That is a real problem. The rest can wait.

"The rack," Rourke says, following your gaze. He lifts the whole roll and drops it on the desk. "Field books, sections, fair sheets. The chainmen give me those, and I cost the faces from them." He turns back to the shutter. "Have a look, if you like. Keep it off the floor; damp ruins the paper, then nobody can read the sections and I get shouted at."

Rourke has the shutter open and a stool set out for you. Apparently that is settled. "Number four's better," he says before you can speak. "Moved the man. Told you." He looks so pleased that you almost forget why you came.

choices.label: Where do the six faces point?

greeting.text: The office has a boarded pane and someone else's tally on the desk. The shutter still opens onto the works; they do not stop for a shutter. Below, full barrows roll past, come back empty, then roll past again.

Rourke watches you climb the ladder again. He says nothing until your head clears the hatch. "Twice," he says. "Everyone saw you twice. Make up your mind about my office. A man who keeps looking at a door will open it eventually, and I'd rather know which day."

choices.label: It's about the works, not the office.

greeting.text: Rourke has the shutter open, one boot on the sill, watching a barrow run. "Number four's slow," he says, as if you've been discussing it all morning. "Been slow since Tuesday. It's the man, not the face. I'll move him tomorrow. He'll be quicker and never know why."

choices.label: Where do the six faces point?

greeting.text: "That," Rourke says, following your gaze, "is bolted through the floor and the joist beneath it. There are eleven pounds in it, Friday's wages." He smiles. "You're the fourth person to look at it that way this year. The other three worked here."

choices.label: Ask him to show you the whole office.

greeting.text: The ladder opens onto the platform. The office is a plank room with a shutter over the whole works. The man at the desk is big, bearded and grey with rock dust. He starts talking before you're through the hatch. "If it's about the pump gallery, Thursday. If it's about the canteen, ask someone else."

choices.label: It's about neither. Show me the works.
Say nothing. Look at the room.

greeting.text: The shutter opens onto the whole works. The overseer leans on the sill with a tally in hand, not looking round. "Number four's slow," he says to no one. Then he turns. "You're not mine. I know all of mine."

he_is_delighted.text: Nobody has ever asked Bael Rourke about the works with any real interest. He's been waiting eleven years for someone to. He shows you the prop pattern and pump schedule, explains why the launder is on the left, what a bucket of sand costs, why there's one on every landing, and why the man who moves one gets docked. He came up through the faces, and tells you so within four minutes.

interjections.text: Kessa, after twenty minutes: "He's still going." Rourke, without stopping: "There's another sixty foot of it, love."
Sera: "He's showing off, not hiding anything. Those look identical from outside, but they're not the same at all."

choices.label: Where do the six faces point?

the_aim_point.text: He unrolls a section and plants his thumb on it. "All six converge here, under the old quarry floor where it came down." He taps the spot twice. "That's a hundred and ten foot of cutting to reach a point about the size of this room. I've costed it four times. It doesn't pay, and I've said so on paper." He rolls it up. "Still, I'm cutting it on time, because that's the instruction."

interjections.text: Ilse: "That's directly under the deep warren. You've taken the floor out from under three thousand people." Rourke: "Two thousand eight hundred. I had them counted. I'm not proud of it, but I had them counted."
Aldric: "What's at the point?" Rourke, plainly: "Rock, brother. Until it isn't."

the_hand_crew.text: "Old workings," Rourke says. For the first time, his face falls. "Past the pumps. There's a crew of four down there with hand tools. No picks, powder or barrows. They take about an inch a week, and that's what they're told to do." He sets down the tally. "I've been twice. I don't go now. I couldn't put it on a return, and I wouldn't know how to word it."

the_wrong_sound.text: "The stone gives back the wrong sound," Rourke says. "That's all. Any face-man will tell you a face has a note. You learn it in a week. That one has no note." He picks up the tally, needing something for his hands. "Fessick's on it. Oldest man I've got, best hands. He asked for the job. I've never understood why."

the_rack_explained.text: "Working paper," Rourke says, then looks at you properly. He takes in your boots, your stance, how many of you there are, and how few have been down a heading. "I tell the clerks this: whoever walks out with that roll will be asked by someone important where they got it and what they mean to do with it. They'd better have an answer that holds up." He turns to the shutter. "You haven't got one yet. Come back after you've been somewhere that makes you harder to argue with, and ask me again."

choices.label: Ask to see the fair sheets anyway.

the_rack_explained.text: "Working paper," Rourke says. "Field books from the chainmen, sections, and the fair sheets drawn from them." He barely glances at it. "The strongbox has the wages, and it's bolted down. That lot's just paper. Anyone who wanted it could carry nine pound of damp paper up two hundred stairs for nothing."

interjections.text: Sera doesn't move or look at the rack again for the rest of the conversation.

he_leaves_you_in_it.text: A barrow saves you the trouble. Number four stops; someone shouts. Rourke swears and takes the ladder two rungs at a time. You're alone in the overseer's office for four minutes, the shutter open and the whole works too busy to look up.

he_gets_wary.text: Rourke stops mid-sentence and studies you. "You've asked me three things about the paper and nothing about the props," he says. "Everybody asks about the props. They're the interesting bit." He closes the section on the desk. He doesn't call for anyone; he doesn't need to. He stands between you and the only ladder, and he came up through the faces.

he_says_a_number.text: He doesn't shout. He leans out of the shutter and calls a number, loud enough to carry over three shifts and a chain-pump. The number brings wardens up the ladder behind you. Then he steps back from the hatch and takes his coat from the nail. It's a good coat, and this is going to get untidy.

everybody_saw.text: You go back down. The platform is where it is, and the shutter faces the works for a reason: a hundred and ninety people saw you go up and come down. By the second bell, there'll be a version of it in the canteen with your face in it.

he_does_not_notice.text: He doesn't notice. He has his back to you at the shutter, counting a barrow run. You leave the overseer's office with three years of someone's work under your coat, past a hundred and ninety people paid by the day who have no reason to look up.

the_room_is_yours.text: It's his office because his name is chalked on the hatch; it's yours because you're standing in it and he isn't. The shutter faces the works. A hundred and ninety people keep working; the bell hasn't gone. The bell is Coyle's, and she's in her hut writing it all in the day book, in the same hand and at the same speed.

sheet_six_here.text: You reach sheet six. Without turning, Rourke says, "That's the valuation. It isn't mine; it comes from downriver so I can cost the haulage against it." He keeps watching number four. "There's a town on that sheet somewhere. Rivermark. I've never been."
